2.title: Four steps, out loud
2.text: On your whiteboard. Say each step out loud as you do it: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Then write the check underneath.

visual.sub: Show your board after each one.

prompts: Solve 552 ÷ 6. Say the four steps out loud as you go.
Write the check under it: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.

notes.do: Whiteboards. He holds up his board after each problem. Do not tap or reveal anything on the laptop; this slide is all whiteboard.
notes.say: These are from last week. Fast and sure, with the check every time.
notes.ask: Why do we start with 55 and not 5?
notes.listen: 552 ÷ 6 = 92 (check 6 × 92 = 552). 552 ÷ 4 = 138 (check 4 × 138 = 552). 6 does not fit into 5, so start with 55.

3.title: Your Practice, fixed
3.text: These three came from your own Lesson 2 Practice. Work each one on your whiteboard first, then answer.

items.q: 437 ÷ 6 = 72 R5. Which multiplication CHECKS this answer?
items.why: To check, multiply the divisor by the quotient, then add the remainder back: 6 × 72 = 432, and 432 + 5 = 437. ✅
no: The remainder was left over, so you ADD it back, not take it away. 432 − 5 = 427, not 437.
Multiply the divisor by the quotient: 6 × 72, not 6 × 5.
The divisor is 6 and the quotient is 72: 6 × 72, then add the remainder 5.

items.q: Someone wrote 83 ÷ 6 = 12 R11. What went wrong?
items.why: A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. 11 is bigger than 6, so one more 6 fits: 11 − 6 = 5. The answer is 13 R5. Check: 6 × 13 + 5 = 83. ✅
no: Look at the remainder. Is 11 smaller than 6?
83 can be divided by 6. It just has a remainder.

items.why: 12 does not fit into 9 even once, so the quotient is 0 and all 9 are left over: 0 R9. Check: 12 × 0 + 9 = 9. ✅
items.no: How many 12s fit into 9? Not even one. So the quotient is 0. What is left over?

notes.do: He works each problem on his whiteboard and shows you BEFORE he taps. He says the rule out loud.
notes.say: These are your three misses from last week's Practice. Today you fix them like a teacher would.
notes.ask: What are the two remainder rules?
notes.listen: 1) In the check, ADD the remainder back. 2) The remainder must be smaller than the divisor. On 9 ÷ 12 he typed .75 last week: in long division the answer is 0 R9.

12.title: A two-digit divisor with a remainder
12.text: Deja's class ends up with 569 cans. Now it is 569 ÷ 24. Use your multiples list: 24 · 48 · 72 · 96 · 120.

items.no: Start with 56. Which multiple of 24 fits under 56?
Multiply 24 × 23 first (you know it: Deja's 552). Then add 17.

items.q: Deja splits 569 cans evenly among 24 pantries. What does the 17 mean?
choices: 17 cans are left over after every pantry gets 23
items.why: Each pantry gets 23 cans, and 17 cans are left over. They cannot be shared evenly, because 17 is less than 24.
no: The remainder is what is left over, not what is missing.

notes.do: Whiteboard first: multiples list at the top, then the long division, then the check. He shows his board before typing.
notes.say: Same four steps, plus the list. And the remainder has to be smaller than 24.
notes.ask: What does the 17 mean in Deja's story?
notes.listen: 23 cans for each pantry, 17 cans left over. If he says 'each pantry gets 17', point back to the quotient.

11.title: Two-digit divisors: 552 ÷ 24
11.text: Back to Deja's real problem. Step 0: make a multiples list for 24. It turns guessing into looking.

steps.text: Divide. 24 does not fit into 5. Look at 55. The list says 48 fits and 72 is too big, so → 2.
Check: 24 × 23 = 552. ✅ Each pantry gets 23 cans. Is 23 between 20 and 30? Yes.

11.tip: With a 2-digit divisor, write the multiples list first. Then each step is just looking it up.

notes.do: He writes the multiples list for 24 across the top of his whiteboard by adding 24 each time, then works 552 ÷ 24 under it as you click through.
notes.say: Same four steps as before. The only new thing is the list.
notes.ask: Why is 2 the first quotient digit and not 3?
notes.listen: 24 × 3 = 72 is more than 55. The biggest multiple that fits under 55 is 48.

10.title: Remainders and the check

visual.text:
Malia writes (for the hamster):
“A class hamster would teach us real responsibility. We'd take turns feeding it, cleaning its cage, and learning about how animals live. My cousin's class had a guinea pig, and everyone learned so much about caring for something besides themselves. It made the whole class feel closer, too.”

Theo writes (against the hamster):
“I love animals, but a classroom isn't the best place for one. Someone has to remember to feed it every single day, including weekends and school breaks. A few kids in our class are allergic to fur, too. I think we should get a class fish tank instead. It's calming, and nobody's allergic to fish.”

items.q: Which is the STRONGEST evidence in Theo's piece?
choices: Theo just does not feel like it
A few kids in the class are allergic to fur
items.why: It is a real fact that would affect students in the class. That makes it strong evidence.
no: Theo never says that. It would only be a feeling anyway.
That is not in his piece, and a feeling is weak evidence.
That is Malia's cousin, and Theo never mentions a cousin.

items.q: Why is Theo's fish tank idea a compromise?
choices: It gives the class a pet but avoids the fur allergy problem
It means the class gets no pet at all
It means Malia wins the vote
Fish tanks are required by the school
items.why: Each side gets something: the class still has a pet (Malia's side), with no fur allergy problem (Theo's side).
no: A fish tank IS a class pet.
Malia wanted a hamster, not a fish tank.
Nothing in the text says that.

items.q: Compare them: Malia and Theo BOTH want the class to have some kind of class ________. Type the word.
items.why: Malia wants a hamster and Theo wants a fish tank, so both want a class pet.
items.no: What do a hamster and a fish tank have in common here?
items.hint: Malia wants a hamster. Theo wants fish.

notes.do: He reads both pieces again and points to the exact sentence for each answer.
notes.ask: Which is stronger evidence: 'my cousin's class loved it' or 'a few kids are allergic'? Why?
notes.listen: Both are real details, but the allergy fact affects students in this class right now, so it weighs more.

15.title: Compare and contrast
15.text: Read Malia's and Theo's pieces again. Strong readers do not just pick a side. They notice what each person cares about most.

visual.text:
Malia writes (for the hamster):
“A class hamster would teach us real responsibility. We'd take turns feeding it, cleaning its cage, and learning about how animals live. My cousin's class had a guinea pig, and everyone learned so much about caring for something besides themselves. It made the whole class feel closer, too.”

Theo writes (against the hamster):
“I love animals, but a classroom isn't the best place for one. Someone has to remember to feed it every single day, including weekends and school breaks. A few kids in our class are allergic to fur, too. I think we should get a class fish tank instead. It's calming, and nobody's allergic to fish.”

steps.text: Compare (same): Both care about the class. Both like animals. Both actually want some kind of class pet.
Contrast (different): Malia wants a hamster; Theo wants a fish tank.
Contrast (different): Malia focuses on what the class would learn. Theo focuses on practical problems: feeding it every day, even on breaks, and fur allergies.
Why? They weigh different things as most important. That is what makes a viewpoint.

15.tip: Use clue words. Same: both, also, alike. Different: but, while, instead.

notes.do: Have him reread both pieces on this slide first. Then a whiteboard T-chart (Same | Different) from the pieces BEFORE you click the steps. This prepares him for Pathways Week 7 Reading on Thursday.
notes.say: Compare is same. Contrast is different. Say a sentence with 'both' and a sentence with 'while.'
notes.ask: Give me one sentence that compares them and one that contrasts them.
notes.listen: 'Both Malia and Theo care about the class.' 'Malia focuses on learning, while Theo focuses on daily care.'
